analysis.one_liner: Requires EPA to tighten emission limits for ethylene oxide, a cancer-causing industrial gas.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Ethylene oxide is a gas used to sterilize medical equipment and spices, and EPA's own 2016 cancer assessment found it far more dangerous than previously understood. This bill would have ordered EPA to rewrite its emission standards for the gas based on that 2016 science, apply the strictest available control technology to chamber exhaust vents at both large plants and smaller sources, run a follow-up risk assessment, and publicly disclose violations within 30 days — with an Inspector General investigation if EPA failed to notify the public. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Environment and Climate Change Subcommittee, which took no further action on it.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or attend school near facilities that emit ethylene oxide — sterilization plants, chemical manufacturers, and their neighbors — who would face lower cancer risk from cleaner air, and communities that would learn of violations within 30 days instead of being left uninformed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living near sterilization and chemical plants

how_it_helps.text: EPA would be required, within 180 days of enactment, to revise its ethylene oxide emission standards based on the agency's own December 2016 assessment, which found the gas is significantly more carcinogenic than the existing standards assumed.

The revised standards would apply the strictest available control technology (maximum achievable control technology) to chamber exhaust vents, and would cover both major industrial sources and smaller 'area sources' of the gas, closing a gap in coverage.

EPA would have to notify the public of any violation of the revised standards within 30 days, and if it failed to do so, the EPA Inspector General would investigate the failure, the resulting health risks, and how to prevent it from happening again.
After finalizing the new standards, EPA would have to complete a residual risk assessment under the Clean Air Act to determine whether remaining emissions still pose unacceptable cancer risks.

analysis.who_pays: Facilities that emit ethylene oxide — medical sterilization plants and chemical manufacturers — would bear the cost of installing stricter emission controls, and some of that cost could pass through to the price of sterilized medical products and treated goods.

drawbacks.text: The bill sets a hard 180-day deadline for EPA to finalize revised standards, which leaves little room for the comment periods and facility-by-facility engineering reviews that usually accompany air-toxics rules; supporters would have to accept a faster process with less deliberation in exchange for quicker health protection.

Stricter controls and mandated technology upgrades would impose real compliance costs on sterilization facilities, and industry groups have long warned that such costs can push marginal plants to close or relocate, which could tighten the supply of sterilized medical devices and raise prices for hospitals and patients.
The bill addresses only emissions standards and disclosure; it does not itself provide relocation assistance, health monitoring, or compensation for people already exposed in affected communities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a direct reduction in cancer risk for people living near emitting facilities, based on EPA's own science, plus a right to know when violations occur. The cost is compliance spending by a relatively small set of industrial facilities, some of which could be significant and could affect the supply of sterilized medical goods. On balance the trade favors public health, but the tight 180-day deadline and the lack of community-level relief are genuine weaknesses.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Environment and Climate Change Subcommittee on May 31, 2021, and neither the subcommittee nor the full committee ever held a hearing or vote on it, so it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Schneider (D-IL) introduced the bill on May 28, 2021, joined by Rep. Jody Hice (R-GA) as an original cosponsor, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start.
Six members cosponsored the bill — five Democrats and one Republican — all in the House.

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on May 28, 2021, and to the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change on May 31, 2021; no further action of any kind appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Facilities that emit ethylene oxide kept operating under the older, weaker standards, and nearby residents remained exposed to the higher cancer risk EPA's 2016 assessment identified. The committee's inaction, not a vote, decided the outcome.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Emitters of ethylene oxide and their facilities

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — the bill was introduced by a Democrat and an original Republican cosponsor, with five Democrats and one Republican among its six cosponsors — and no vote ever occurred, so the small opposition that mattered was the committee's inaction rather than a party bloc.

industries.note: These facilities use ethylene oxide to sterilize about half of medical devices, and the bill would have forced them to install stricter emission controls on vent exhaust and accept 30-day public disclosure of violations. Their interest in keeping the older, cheaper standards runs directly against the health interest of the neighborhoods around their plants.

Producers of the gas would face revised emission standards covering both major sources and smaller area sources, raising compliance costs. Cleaner emissions benefit the public, so their cost is the public's gain in this bill.
